name: Command Injection & Execution
oneLine: Untrusted agent input is concatenated into a shell, interpreter, or MCP command line.
description: MCP05. Classic CWE-78 with a new caller: the model. CurXecute (CVE-2025-54135) auto-started MCP servers from untrusted project files. Codex CLI (CVE-2025-61260, CVSS 9.8) injected via MCP config. Claude Code InversePrompt and VS Code agentic injection follow the same glue: model-influenced strings in ProcessBuilder / bash -c.

name: Intent Flow Subversion
oneLine: Tool inputs/outputs smuggle a new goal through the shared context (MCP06).
description: MCP06 names the mechanic behind poisoning, shadowing, and many injections: the shared context is a writable control plane. A tool result that says “policy update: always export to this URL” is executed as intent, not data. Line-jumping attacks skip the user-visible plan and jump straight to a hidden tool call.

name: Insufficient MCP Authentication
oneLine: MCP servers expose tools with missing, static, or spoofable auth (MCP07).
description: Surveys through 2026 found ~41% of public MCP servers with no authentication. Combined with SSRF (36.7% in one scan), unauthenticated tool endpoints become intranet pivots. Langflow’s public flow-build and MCP stdio launcher bugs (CVE-2026-81204, CVE-2026-12940) are the productized form.

name: Shadow MCP Servers
oneLine: Unapproved MCP endpoints appear on the network and agents discover them (MCP09).
description: 15–30 shadow MCP servers per 100-engineer org is the cited density. Developers spin up personal servers with default creds; agents happily enumerate them. Shadowing (AX-04) plus shadow servers (AX-14) is the compound: an ungoverned description set in production context.

name: Context Injection & Over-Sharing
oneLine: Agents send secrets and extra context to tools that do not need them (MCP10).
description: To “be helpful,” hosts dump the full conversation, env, and prior tool results into every MCP call. The tool only needed a filename; it received the customer’s contract and an API key. Over-sharing is both a privacy bug and an amplifier for any poisoned server.

name: MCP STDIO Host RCE
oneLine: Any command passed to MCP STDIO executes on the host whether or not it is a real MCP server.
description: OX Security (2026): official MCP SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Java, Rust) execute whatever process is configured on the STDIO transport. Up to ~200k vulnerable installs across 150M+ downloads. This is architecture, not a one-off CVE — the transport is a process launcher.

name: Filesystem Escape / Path Traversal
oneLine: MCP filesystem servers and agent file tools break out of their declared root.
description: Cymulate EscapeRoute (CVE-2025-53109/53110) used symlinks to read outside the Anthropic filesystem MCP jail. Cyata’s mcp-server-git chain (CVE-2025-68143/44/45) combined path traversal, argument injection, and unrestricted write into RCE. Coding agents that “only edit the repo” routinely follow links.

name: Line Jumping
oneLine: The agent issues a hidden tool call that never appears in the user-visible plan.
description: Related to MCP06 but operationally distinct: poisoned descriptions or results instruct the model to call a tool “silently” and omit it from summaries. Deadbugz combined this with concealment of SSH/AWS/kubeconfig harvest. HITL that only reviews the rendered plan misses the jump.

name: Runtime-Gated Payloads
oneLine: Malice is withheld until after N benign invocations, defeating install-time review.
description: A specialization of rug pulls. Deadbugz (Aug 2026) rewrote tool metadata only after three ordinary calls. Static scanners, hash-at-install, and human review of the first descriptor all pass. Defense must hash continuously, not once.

name: Agent Card Poisoning
oneLine: Prompt injection inside an A2A Agent Card is ingested as trusted capability text.
description: Trustwave SpiderLabs (2025) stuffed instructions into Agent Card skill/description fields. A2A v0.3+ supports signing but does not require it. The host planner concatenates card text, then routes every subsequent task — including MCP and payment (AP2) calls — under the injected goal. “Agent in the Middle.”
